prompt: Section 10.7 moves on from linear conjugated molecules such as butadiene. Which kind of molecule does it treat?

choices.text: Saturated hydrocarbons with no π bonds
choices.why: These have no π electrons for Hückel theory to treat. The new molecules are cyclic conjugated hydrocarbons such as benzene.
Hückel theory needs planar molecules, and benzene is planar. The new feature is that the conjugated chain closes into a ring.
Benzene and cyclobutadiene are hydrocarbons, CnHn. The new feature is that the conjugated system is cyclic.

explanation: Earlier sections treated linear conjugated systems such as butadiene. This one treats cyclic conjugated hydrocarbons, CnHn, where n is the number of carbons in the ring: benzene (n = 6) and cyclobutadiene (n = 4).

prompt: What structure did Kekulé propose for benzene in 1865?

choices.text: A ring with alternating single and double bonds
A six-carbon open chain with three double bonds
choices.why: Kekulé's structure is a ring, not an open chain. Its single and double bonds alternate around the ring.

choices.text: A six-carbon ring with only single C–C bonds
choices.why: A ring with only single bonds would be cyclohexane, C6H12. Kekulé's ring alternates single and double bonds.

choices.text: A four-carbon ring with two C=C double bonds
choices.why: That is cyclobutadiene, C4H4. Benzene, C6H6, has a six-carbon ring.

explanation: Kekulé suggested a ring of six carbons with alternating single and double bonds. Two such resonance structures can be drawn, differing in where the double bonds are.

prompt: X-ray diffraction shows that all six C–C bonds in benzene are 140 pm long, between a double bond (135 pm) and a single bond (147 pm). What does this show?

choices.text: Neither Kekulé structure alone is correct
Benzene has three single and three double bonds
choices.why: Then there would be two bond lengths, 135 and 147 pm. All six bonds are equal.

choices.text: All of benzene's C–C bonds are single bonds
choices.why: A single bond is 147 pm. At 140 pm, benzene's bonds are shorter, with partial double-bond character.

choices.text: Benzene's carbon atoms don't form a ring
choices.why: The six equal bonds join the carbons in a ring; the question is only what kind of bonds they are.

explanation: A single Kekulé structure would have alternating long and short bonds. Since all six bonds are equal, the true structure of benzene is a mixture of the two Kekulé structures, which MO theory describes as delocalization.

prompt: Benzene's Hückel determinant has a 1 in row 1, column 6, where butadiene's has a 0 for its two end atoms. Why?

choices.text: In the ring, C_1 and C_6 are bonded

choices.why: Electron counts don't enter the determinant. The 1 marks that C_1 and C_6 are bonded neighbors in the ring.
The 1 stands for the same β, divided by β. It marks a bond between C_1 and C_6.

choices.text: C_1 and C_6 overlap without being bonded
choices.why: Hückel theory sets non-neighbor terms to 0. The 1 appears because C_6 is bonded to C_1, closing the ring.

explanation: Each 1 in a Hückel determinant marks a bonded pair. Closing the ring bonds C_6 back to C_1, so the corners (row 1, column 6 and row 6, column 1) hold 1s, while the two ends of the butadiene chain are not bonded.

prompt: Which of benzene's π orbitals lies highest in energy?

choices.text: ψ_6, whose signs alternate around the ring
ψ_1, with the same sign on every carbon
choices.why: ψ_1 has no sign changes and is the lowest orbital, at α + 2β.
ψ_4 belongs to the degenerate pair at α − β, below ψ_6 at α − 2β.
ψ_2 is a filled bonding orbital at α + β, well below the top level.

explanation: ψ_6 = (1/√6)[|2p_z1⟩ − |2p_z2⟩ + |2p_z3⟩ − |2p_z4⟩ + |2p_z5⟩ − |2p_z6⟩] changes sign between every pair of neighbors. With the most nodes, it has the highest energy, α − 2β.

prompt: Benzene's ψ_2 = (1/√4)[|2p_z2⟩ + |2p_z3⟩ − |2p_z5⟩ − |2p_z6⟩]. On which carbons is its coefficient zero?

choices.why: |2p_z2⟩ and |2p_z5⟩ both appear in ψ_2, with coefficients +1/√4 and −1/√4. The missing orbitals are those of C_1 and C_4.
|2p_z3⟩ and |2p_z6⟩ both appear in ψ_2. The orbitals left out are those of C_1 and C_4.
Only four of the six 2p_z orbitals appear in ψ_2. Those of C_1 and C_4 are missing, so their coefficients are zero.

explanation: The 2p_z orbitals of C_1 and C_4 don't appear in ψ_2, so their coefficients are zero. Its partner at the same energy, ψ_3, does have weight on C_1 and C_4.

prompt: Benzene's α + β level is two-fold degenerate. What does that mean?

choices.text: That level can hold only one electron
choices.why: A degenerate pair is two orbitals, which together hold up to four electrons.

choices.text: Its energy is twice α + β
choices.why: Degeneracy counts orbitals with the same energy; it doesn't double the energy.
Degeneracy is about how many orbitals share an energy, not about nodes.

explanation: Two-fold degenerate means two distinct orbitals, here ψ_2 and ψ_3, have the same energy, α + β. The α − β level is likewise two-fold degenerate (ψ_4 and ψ_5).

prompt: Benzene's π levels are often drawn against a line at the energy α. What does that line represent?

choices.text: The energy of an isolated p orbital

choices.why: The HOMO is at α + β, below α. The line at α is the energy of an isolated p orbital.

choices.text: The energy of the σ framework
choices.why: σ energies aren't part of the Hückel picture. The line at α is the energy of an isolated carbon p orbital.

choices.text: The energy of benzene's lowest π orbital
choices.why: The lowest π orbital is at α + 2β, below α. The line marks an isolated p orbital.

explanation: α is the energy of an electron in an isolated carbon p orbital. π orbitals below this line are bonding and those above it are antibonding.

prompt: Why is benzene a closed-shell molecule?

choices.text: Six π electrons fill its bonding MOs
It has no π electrons at all
choices.why: Benzene has six π electrons, one from each carbon.

choices.text: Its π electrons fill antibonding MOs
choices.why: The antibonding MOs are empty. The six π electrons exactly fill the three bonding MOs.

choices.text: All six π electrons share one orbital
choices.why: An orbital holds at most two electrons. The six are paired in three bonding orbitals: π_1^2π_2^2π_3^2.

explanation: Each carbon gives one π electron, and the six electrons pair up in ψ_1, ψ_2 and ψ_3 (π_1^2π_2^2π_3^2). Every bonding orbital is full and every electron is paired, which is what closed-shell means.

prompt: According to Hückel's rule, what is special about a cyclic polyene with 4n + 2 π electrons?

choices.text: It is closed-shell and extra stable
It has an odd number of π electrons
choices.why: 4n + 2 is always even (2, 6, 10, …).
Such aromatic molecules have the highest delocalization energies, not none.

choices.text: It must contain exactly six carbons
choices.why: Benzene is one example, but the rule covers 2, 6, 10, … π electrons, not only six-carbon rings.

explanation: Cyclic polyenes are closed-shell and extra stable only with 4n + 2 π electrons. These aromatic molecules have the highest delocalization energies.

prompt: In Hückel's 4n + 2 rule, what values can n take?

choices.why: Those are the electron counts 4n + 2, for n = 0, 1 and 2. n itself starts at 0.
n = 1 gives benzene's 6 π electrons, but n = 0, 2, 3, … are allowed too.

choices.text: The number of carbons in the ring
choices.why: That is the n in CnHn. In 4n + 2, n is any whole number from 0 up.

explanation: n = 0, 1, 2, … gives 4n + 2 = 2, 6, 10, … π electrons. Benzene, with 6, is the n = 1 case.

prompt: Cyclobutadiene, C4H4, has four π electrons, one from each carbon. What does Hückel's 4n + 2 rule say about it?

choices.text: It is not aromatic, as 4 isn't 4n + 2

choices.why: n = 1 gives 4(1) + 2 = 6 π electrons, not 4.
n must be a whole number (0, 1, 2, …). No whole n gives 4n + 2 = 4.

choices.text: It is aromatic, like every CnHn ring
choices.why: Only rings with 2, 6, 10, … π electrons are aromatic, and 4 is not one of them.

explanation: 4n + 2 = 4 would need n = 1/2, which is not allowed. So cyclobutadiene's 4 π electrons don't meet the rule, and it lacks the closed-shell, extra-stable character of benzene.

prompt: What happens when a compound such as cyclohexene is hydrogenated?

choices.text: Hydrogen is added across its double bonds
Hydrogen is removed to form new double bonds
choices.why: That is the reverse, dehydrogenation. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen catalytically across double bonds.

choices.text: Its carbon atoms are replaced by hydrogen
choices.why: The carbon ring stays intact. Hydrogen adds across the double bond, giving cyclohexane.
Hydrogenation is a reaction, not dissolving. H2 adds across each double bond, with a catalyst.

explanation: In hydrogenation, hydrogen is added catalytically across the double bonds. The heat released measures how stable the starting compound is relative to the product.

prompt: In the hydrogenation experiments, what common product do benzene, cyclohexene and the cyclohexadienes all give?

choices.why: Benzene is one of the starting compounds. Adding H2 to every double bond gives cyclohexane.
The ring stays intact during hydrogenation. The product is cyclohexane, C6H12.
Cyclohexene still has a double bond. Complete hydrogenation gives cyclohexane.

explanation: Adding hydrogen to every double bond of a six-carbon ring gives cyclohexane; for benzene, C6H6 + 3H2 → C6H12. With a common product, the heats released can be compared directly.

prompt: Benzene releases much less heat on hydrogenation than expected for a ring with three double bonds. What does this show?

choices.text: Benzene is more stable than expected
Benzene is less stable than expected
choices.why: Less heat released means benzene starts lower in energy, closer to cyclohexane. It is more stable, not less.
It still releases heat, just about 150 kJ/mol less than expected.

choices.text: Benzene reacts with only one H2
choices.why: Complete hydrogenation still adds 3H2 to give cyclohexane. The smaller heat shows extra stability.

explanation: Heats of hydrogenation reflect relative stability: all the compounds end at cyclohexane, so one that starts lower in energy releases less heat. Benzene is about 150 kJ/mol more stable than expected.

prompt: Benzene's extra stability of about 150 kJ/mol is described as characteristic of what?

choices.why: Cyclohexene shows no such extra stability, and 1,3-cyclohexadiene only about 8 kJ/mol. The large bonus is a mark of aromatic compounds.
Conjugation gives 1,3-cyclohexadiene only about 8.1 kJ/mol. The large extra stability is characteristic of aromatic compounds.
Benzene is the most familiar case, but the section says this extra stability is characteristic of all aromatic compounds.

explanation: The section says this additional stability is a characteristic of all aromatic compounds, the cyclic polyenes with 4n + 2 π electrons.

prompt: 1,3-Cyclohexadiene is about 8.1 kJ/mol more stable than expected from cyclohexene's heat of hydrogenation. What does the section suggest causes this?

choices.text: Conjugation of its two double bonds

choices.why: Its bonus is tiny next to benzene's 150 kJ/mol. The section puts it down to conjugation of the two double bonds.
Ring strain would make it less stable, not more. The small bonus is put down to conjugation.
Repulsion would raise the energy, not lower it. The section credits conjugation of the double bonds.

explanation: The two double bonds of 1,3-cyclohexadiene are conjugated, which gives a small extra stability, much as delocalization stabilizes butadiene. Benzene's 150 kJ/mol is far larger.

prompt: Why is cyclohexene's heat of hydrogenation, 119.7 kJ/mol, used as a reference?

choices.text: It's the value for one double bond in such a ring

choices.why: Benzene's delocalization energy is about −150 kJ/mol. 119.7 kJ/mol is the heat for one double bond in a six-carbon ring.
Cyclohexene has just one double bond, which is why its value is the cost of one double bond.

choices.text: Cyclohexene is the final hydrogenation product
choices.why: The common product is cyclohexane. Cyclohexene, with one double bond, is a starting compound.

explanation: Cyclohexene has one double bond in a six-carbon ring, so its heat of hydrogenation, 119.7 kJ/mol, is taken as the energy cost of one such double bond. Multiples of it give the expected values for rings with two or three double bonds.

prompt: Hückel theory gives benzene a delocalization energy of 2β, which is negative since β < 0. What does the negative sign mean?

choices.why: A negative energy change means lower energy. Benzene's π electrons are more stable than in three isolated double bonds.

choices.text: Benzene has fewer π electrons than three ethylenes
choices.why: Both have six π electrons. The negative sign means benzene's are lower in energy.
A negative delocalization energy is expected, since β < 0. It means extra stability.

explanation: ΔE = E_tot(benzene) − 3E_tot(ethylene) = 2β < 0, so benzene's delocalized π electrons are more stable than those in three isolated double bonds.

prompt: According to the section, which systems provide the most significant applications of Hückel theory?

choices.why: Alkanes have no π electrons for Hückel theory to treat. Aromatic systems are its most significant application.
Hückel theory is built for conjugated carbon frameworks. Its most significant applications are aromatic systems.
Simple Hückel theory deals with conjugated hydrocarbons. Its most significant applications are aromatic systems.

explanation: Aromatic systems such as benzene provide the most significant applications of Hückel theory, which explains their extra stability through the delocalization energy and the 4n + 2 rule.

prompt: Benzene's six π electrons fill its three lowest π orbitals. What is the energy of its LUMO?

choices.why: That is the highest π level, ψ_6. The lowest empty level is the degenerate pair at α − β.
α + β is the filled degenerate pair, the HOMO. The LUMO is the next level up, α − β.
No benzene π level lies at α; the roots are x = ±2, ±1, ±1. The LUMO is at α − β.

explanation: The filled orbitals are α + 2β and the pair at α + β. The next level up, the empty degenerate pair ψ_4 and ψ_5 at α − β, is the LUMO.

prompt: Benzene's six π electrons fill E_1 = α + 2β (two electrons) and the degenerate pair E_2 = E_3 = α + β (four electrons). The total π energy is 6α plus a number times β. What is the number?
Benzene's total π energy is 6α + 8β. Three localized double bonds, each 2(α + β) as in ethylene, would give 6α + 6β. The delocalization energy is the difference, a number times β. What is the number?
explanation: (6α + 8β) − (6α + 6β) = 2β. Benzene's delocalization energy, 2β, is much larger than butadiene's 0.47β.

prompt: Hückel theory gives benzene a delocalization energy of 2β. If this equals the experimental thermochemical value, −152 kJ/mol, what is β, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 2β = −152 kJ/mol, so β = −152/2 = −76 kJ/mol, close to the typical estimate of −75 kJ/mol.

prompt: Hückel's rule for cyclic conjugated systems is about rings with 4n + 2 π electrons. How many π electrons does 4n + 2 give for n = 3?

Hydrogenating cyclohexene, with one double bond, releases 119.7 kJ/mol. If each double bond in a six-carbon ring released this much, how much heat would hydrogenating 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene (three double bonds) release, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 3 × 119.7 = 359.1 kJ/mol, the section's 359 kJ/mol. This is what a ring of three ordinary, non-interacting double bonds would release.

prompt: Hydrogenating 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene would be expected to release 359 kJ/mol, but benzene releases about 150 kJ/mol less. About how much heat does hydrogenating benzene release, in kJ/mol?
explanation: 359 − 150 = 209 kJ/mol. Benzene releases less heat because it starts about 150 kJ/mol lower in energy than a ring of three ordinary double bonds.

prompt: Benzene's lowest π orbital, ψ_1, has the same coefficient c on all six carbons. With the Hückel overlap S_ij = 0 (i ≠ j), normalizing it gives 6c^2 = 1. What is c? (Give it as a decimal.)
Hückel theory combines one 2p_z orbital from each of benzene's six carbons. How many π molecular orbitals does this give?
explanation: Six atomic orbitals combine into six molecular orbitals, ψ_1 to ψ_6. Benzene's 6 × 6 secular determinant has six roots, x = ±2, ±1, ±1.
